Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01An exact solution need not be a regular black hole Stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum solutions need not be Kerr. In the Tomimatsu–Sato family, labelled by an integer δ, δ = 1 is Kerr. Focus on δ = 2 and read physical differences from its supplied Ernst potential. The assumptions differ from black-hole uniqueness theorems requiring a regular horizon. G = c = 1, p²+q² = 1, p > 0, |q| < 1 ρ = κ√[(x²−1)(1−y²)], z = κxy M = 2κ/p, J = M²q Here x > 1 and −1 ≤ y ≤ 1 are prolate spheroidal coordinates; ρ is a cylindrical coordinate, not a material density. M denotes the geometrized mass GM/c². The δ = 2 normalization differs from Kerr’s M = κ/p, so equal x values do not mean equal physical radii. 02Specify the solution with a complex potential Write the stationary axisymmetric vacuum field using the Ernst potential ℰ = f + iψ, where f = −gₜₜ and ψ is the twist potential. Supply the following polynomial solution. Complex arithmetic uses i² = −1; modulus and complex conjugation are not ordinary real squaring. ℰ = (A−B)/(A+B) A = p²(x⁴−1)+q²(y⁴−1)−2ipqxy(x²−y²) B = 2px(x²−1)+2iqy(y²−1) The vacuum equations reduce to the complex PDE below, taken as the supplied field equation. The right side uses complex squares of derivatives, not squared moduli. Numerical checks compare finite-difference residuals away from singularities and f computed from an independent metric representation. Re(ℰ){∂x[(x²−1)∂xℰ]+∂y[(1−y²)∂yℰ]} = (x²−1)(∂xℰ)²+(1−y²)(∂yℰ)² 03Read the quadrupole from axis data On the upper axis y = 1, z = κx. Form ξ = (1−ℰ)/(1+ℰ) = B/A and cancel the common factor. In its asymptotic 1/z expansion, the first three coefficients give M, iJ, and the mass quadrupole Q in this convention. Higher coefficients cannot all be identified directly with relativistic multipoles. ξaxis = 2px/[p²(x²+1)−2ipqx] = 2/(px)+4iq/(p²x²)−[2/p+8q²/p³]/x³+O(x−4) = M/z+iJ/z²+Q/z³+O(z−4) QTS2/M³ = −(1+3q²)/4 QKerr/M³ = −q² (QTS2−QKerr)/M³ = −(1−q²)/4 At fixed M and J, hence fixed q, the quadrupoles differ. Nonrotating TS2 retains Q = −M³/4 and is not spherical. The sign follows Manko’s equation (10). Do not translate this relativistic quadrupole directly into the axis ratio of a homogeneous Newtonian spheroid. 04Locate the ring singularity For 0 < |q| < 1 on y = 0, the condition A+B = 0 locates a ring singularity with x > 1. The polynomial below increases monotonically for x > 1, is −q² at one, and becomes positive at infinity. The panel finds its unique root by bisection. p²x₀⁴+2px₀(x₀²−1)−1 = 0 ρring/M = (p/2)√(x₀²−1) At q = 0 the root retreats to the boundary x = 1; the exterior-ring interpretation no longer applies. TS2 also has causal pathologies including closed timelike curves. It is not automatically an alternative model of an ordinary rotating black hole. This lesson computes the ring location without reconstructing the full causal diagram or all geodesics. 05Compare at fixed mass and spin Multipoles and ring coordinates are recomputed theoretical quantities. A singular ring is neither a black-hole shadow nor a material ring. Spin q is continuous, whereas δ labels integer solution families; parameter comparison is not time evolution. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Does the δ = 2 spacetime become Schwarzschild at q = 0? Show the answer and reasoning No. Q/M³ = −1/4 remains: it is static but nonspherical. At δ = 1, q = 0 instead gives Schwarzschild. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization.
